title: Egg Drop Soup
subtitle: Light chicken broth thickened with cornflour and finished with silken egg ribbons
excerpt: A cornflour slurry thickens the broth just enough for the egg to autumn in ribbons rather than scraps. The whole soup takes under 15 minutes and relies entirely on good stock. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Dan hua tang (egg flower soup) is one of the most widely eaten soups in Chinese home cooking, appearing in regional variations across Cantonese, Shanghainese, and Sichuan cuisine. The technique of streaming beaten egg into hot, starch-thickened stock to create ribbon-like 'egg flowers' is documented in Chinese culinary literature from the Song dynasty. The dish was introduced to Western audiences through early Chinese-American restaurant menus and remains one of the best-known Chinese soups globally.

content.text: This serves 4 and takes under 15 minutes. The
egg flower technique
-- pouring a thin stream of beaten egg into hot, starch-thickened broth while stirring -- creates long, silken ribbons rather than scrambled-egg chunks. The
cornflour slurry
is what makes this possible: the viscosity slows the egg as it hits the liquid, keeping the ribbons intact.
Good
chicken stock

is the foundation. The soup has so few ingredients that a watery stock will give a thin, flat result. Use a well-seasoned homemade or shop-bought stock. The slurry goes in before the egg -- if you reverse the order, the egg disperses into scraps and the soup looks broken.
What you need
Method
Pour the chicken stock into a medium saucepan. Add the ginger slices and bring to a gentle boil over medium heat. Simmer for 3 minutes to infuse, then remove the ginger.

Add the light soy sauce and taste the stock. Season with salt. The stock should be well-seasoned before the egg and cornflour go in -- it is difficult to adjust afterwards without disrupting the ribbons.

Stir the cornflour slurry to recombine (cornflour settles quickly). Bring the stock to a steady simmer, then pour the slurry into the stock in a steady stream, stirring constantly. The soup should thicken within 30 seconds to a lightly viscous consistency -- it should flow easily but coat the back of a spoon.

Stir the soup in one direction to create a slow, circular current. Hold the bowl of beaten egg 20-30 cm above the soup and pour it in a very thin, steady stream into the swirling broth. The egg will set in long ribbons as it hits the hot liquid. Do not stir for 10 seconds after the egg is in -- this allows the ribbons to set.
Give the soup one gentle stir to ensure the egg ribbons are evenly distributed. Add the white pepper. Drizzle the
sesame oil
over the surface.
Ladle into bowls immediately. Scatter sliced spring onions over each bowl. Serve with steamed rice or as the opening course of a larger Chinese meal.

items.symptom: Egg is in small flecks rather than ribbons
items.cause: Egg was poured too fast, the soup was not swirling, or the slurry was insufficient
items.fix: Pour egg from a height in the thinnest possible stream. Stir the soup first to create a current. Make sure the cornflour has visibly thickened the broth before adding egg.

items.symptom: Soup is gluey and too thick
items.cause: Too much cornflour slurry was added
items.fix: Add cornflour slurry gradually, stopping as soon as the soup reaches a lightly viscous consistency. If already over-thickened, add a splash of hot stock to loosen.

items.cause: Soup was stirred too vigorously immediately after adding egg
items.fix: Wait 10 seconds after adding the egg before stirring. Use one gentle fold rather than a vigorous stir.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Dan hua tang appears at the Chinese table as both an everyday home soup and a restaurant staple. In Cantonese cooking it is often served as the final dish of a meal, a light and warming finish after richer courses. In northern Chinese home cooking it serves as a quick weekday soup made from whatever stock is available. The name -- literally 'egg flower soup' -- refers to the way the egg sets in the hot broth in shapes that resemble chrysanthemum petals, a form that Cantonese cooks consider as much an aesthetic achievement as a culinary one.
